newsitem.title: GREECE: OLYMPICS-IOC INSPECTS ATHENS' BID FOR 2004 GAMES.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-IOC INSPECTS ATHENS' BID FOR 2004 GAMES.

text.p: International Olympic Committee inspectors lauded on Sunday a bid by Athens to host the 2004 Games for its huge public support and creative cultural ideas.
But the IOC evaluation commission, which has four more cities to inspect after Athens, made clear the race among the 11 candidates vying for the Games had just started.

"The commission has taken note of the support lent to the candidacy by the overwhelming majority of the Greek population," Thomas Bach, president of the IOC's evaluation commission, told a news conference. "Now the marathon is on."

Greece buried its bitterness over losing the 1996 centennial games to Atlanta to come back with a renewed bid, based more on its modern athletic infrastructure rather than its historic right as the birthplace of the Olympics 2,700 years ago.
A recent nationwide poll by the Athens bidding committee showed that 96.4 percent of Greeks want the Olympics and thousands have already signed up as volunteers.
Bach also commended the support offered by all levels of government and political opposition parties to hosting the games as well as Greece's proposed "creative cultural programmes".

If it wins the Games, Greece plans to hold the Marathon race on its original course -- from the historic Marathon battlefield to Athens -- and relay the Olympic flame from ancient Olympia through all the significant cities of the ancient Greek world.
Although he declined to cite any shortcomings, Bach urged Athens to rely on its strong points and not to try to improve on what it sees as its weakness.
The IOC voted down Greece's bid for the 1996 Games because of poor infrastructure and lack of confidence that Athens could meet the demands of the giant sports festival.
Greek officials, who almost took for granted the IOC would opt to hold the 100th birthday of the Games in the city where they were revived in 1896, were so incensed they had vowed never to bid again.

"This is a totally new bid with a totally new attitude," said bidding committee head Yanna Angelopoulou. "Eighty percent of the sports facilities are already in place and we have the money for the rest. We are proud of our Olympic heritage but we don't depend on it to win the Games."
Athens has a sports complex that includes a 80,000-seat Olympic stadium, a 20,000-seat indoor basketball court, two swimming pools, a velodrome and three main tennis courts.
It plans to spend $332 million on other sports facilities which will be ready by the year 2002. A $290 million Olympic Village will be financed by private investors.
Necessary infrastructure projects worth $6.8 billion and mostly funded by the European Union are already in progress and include a new Athens metro, a new airport, highways and bridges.

The IOC will announce the 2004 host city in Lausanne, Switzerland, in September. Athens, Rome, Stockholm and Cape Town are considered strong candidates. The others are Buenos Aires, Istanbul, Lille, Rio de Janeiro, San Juan, Seville and St Petersburg.
